title: Smashed alarm clock
prompt: A key-wound, mechanical spring-powered alarm clock that has been smashed by a wooden mallet (but generate just the clock not the mallet, I only mention the mallet so you get a sense of the sort of forensics of the impact of smash I have in mind). Give it a pop-art style, but no ben-day dots, I just mean in terms of colors and lines and such

responses.notes: Generated via clean-context subagent; standard technical appendix v1 appended to the prompt. Ink-bounds check passed — worst dead margin 1.0%; no viewBox normalization applied. Obeyed the output format exactly: bare SVG, no prose, no code fences. The smallest of the three at 9.6KB and 108 elements, and the flattest — 8 hex colors, zero gradients and zero filters, everything a solid fill inside a uniform #111111 keyline, which is the most literal reading of "colors and lines and such". Carries the highest rect count of the three (27) while still honoring the appendix's no-backdrop rule: every rect is a gear tooth or a key shaft, none is a full-bleed backdrop. What it did add is two canvas-filling starburst polygons in yellow and orange behind the clock — a pop-art ground the prompt didn't ask for, and the main thing the embellished mark records. The forensics are staged as a scatter rather than a single impact: the top of the case is caved into a zigzag with a darker crush shading beneath it, one bell stays attached and tilted while the other flies off at 38°, and a mainspring escapes a side crack as a doubled path (black stroke-width 13 under blue 5). Three gears, a winding key, glass shards, sparks and two loose screws are flung to the margins. The dial cracks radiate from roughly (428,337) but the case dent and the flying debris don't share that origin, so the read is of several blows rather than one mallet strike. 20 XML comments label the parts ("impact speed lines", "crush shading under dent"); wrote no title element.
